extracted.intended_audience: journalism students, media scholars, practicing journalists and editors
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria about how individual journalists' characteristics, professional roles, and ethical codes influence news content; includes professionalization criteria, role conceptions, and the Society of Professional Journalists Code of Ethics. Useful for assessing journalistic practice, newsroom policy, and media-content influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Influence of communicators' characteristics, backgrounds, and experiences
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no direct influence of communicators' characteristics, backgrounds, and experiences on media content, but content may be affected to the extent that such factors influence both personal and professional attitudes and roles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes variables such as education, gender, ethnicity, and socio-economic background; these factors shape worldview and selection/coverage decisions indirectly (see Figure 5.2). Empirical findings are mixed; organizational routines may suppress or mediate these influences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Influence of personal attitudes, values, and beliefs
rubrics_metrics.description: Communicators' personal attitudes, values, and beliefs can affect their work, though empirical tests produce conflicting results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Shoemaker (1984) found journalists' deviance perceptions correlated with less legitimate coverage; Rainville & McCormick (1977) found racial prejudice affected announcers' descriptions; Pasadeos & Renfro (1988) showed owner influence after Rupert Murdoch's purchase. Influence is more likely when communicators have more power over messages and work under fewer constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional roles / role conceptions (interpretive, dissemination, adversary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists' self-conceived professional roles shape content: interpretive (investigate/analyze), dissemination (get information out quickly/wide audience), adversary (serve as adversary to government/business).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weaver and Wilhoit identified that most journalists score high on the interpretive and dissemination scales; only a minority highly value the adversary role. Role conception affects story style: 'neutrals' (disseminators) produce faster, less interpretive accounts; 'participants' (interpreters) pursue investigation and analysis. Empirical evidence: student reporters identifying as neutrals wrote less fair/comprehensive stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professionalization criteria (what defines a profession)
rubrics_metrics.description: A profession is characterized (Lambeth, 1986) by: (1) full-time occupation; (2) deep commitment to professional goals; (3) governance by a formal organization with professional standards; (4) prescribed formal schooling and specialized knowledge; (5) serving society; (6) high degree of autonomy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied to journalism: journalism meets some but not all criteria (no licensing authority, variable formal schooling, limited autonomy). Use these criteria to assess how 'professional' journalism is and how that affects legitimacy, standards, and content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Socialization to organizational norms
rubrics_metrics.description: New journalists learn on the job—'by osmosis'—what their organization wants through observation, reading their outlet, editing feedback, gossip, and implicit signs from superiors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy is often conveyed indirectly; the editing process provides direct feedback (e.g., editors deleting certain content signals disapproval). Socialization aligns journalists with organizational values and routines that shape selection and framing of news.

rubrics_metrics.name: SPJ Code of Ethics — I. Responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The public's right to know of events of public importance and interest is the overriding mission of the mass media; distributing news and enlightened opinion serves the general welfare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists who use professional status for selfish or unworthy motives violate public trust. Use the 'public's right to know' as primary justification for newsgathering but weigh against other ethical considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: SPJ Code of Ethics — II. Freedom of the Press
rubrics_metrics.description: Freedom of the press is to be guarded as an inalienable right; it carries with it the freedom and responsibility to discuss, question, and challenge government and institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists should uphold unpopular opinions and the privilege to agree with majority, defending the role to speak and challenge public institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: SPJ Code of Ethics — III. Ethics (conflict-of-interest and professional conduct rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists must be free of obligation to any interest other than the public's right to know the truth. Specific rules include: (1) avoid gifts/favors/privileges that compromise integrity; (2) avoid secondary employment/political involvement that compromises integrity; (3) substantiate news communications from private sources before publishing; (4) seek news that serves the public interest and assure public records are open; (5) protect confidential sources; (6) prohibit plagiarism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these concrete prohibitions and expectations to decisions about accepting freebies, outside work, publishing unsubstantiated materials, protecting sources, and attribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: SPJ Code of Ethics — IV. Accuracy and Objectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Good faith with the public is foundational. Truth is the ultimate goal; objectivity is a performance standard to strive for; no excuse for inaccuracies or lack of thoroughness; headlines/photographs must be warranted by content; distinguish news reports from opinion; informed analysis must come from qualified individuals; advocacy pieces should be labeled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these items to evaluate factual accuracy, thoroughness, headline/veracity alignment, labeling of opinion/advocacy, and sourcing of analysis/commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: SPJ Code of Ethics — V. Fair Play
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists must show respect for dignity, privacy, rights, and well-being of people encountered; should not communicate unofficial charges affecting reputation without chance to reply; guard against invading privacy; not pander to morbid curiosity; promptly correct errors; be accountable to public and foster open dialogue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply when considering naming victims, publishing allegations, graphic content, privacy intrusions, correction policies, and community engagement mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: SPJ Code of Ethics — VI. Mutual Trust
rubrics_metrics.description: Adherence to the code intends to preserve and strengthen mutual trust between journalists and the public; the Society will encourage adherence and the framing of organizational codes of ethics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use to justify training, codes, and institutional reinforcement of ethical practice; evaluate whether an outlet fosters mutual trust through policies and education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethics Handbook guiding principles and ten-question decision framework
rubrics_metrics.description: Guiding principles: 'Seek truth and report is as fully as possible; act independently; and minimize harm.' Asked to use ten sets of questions when assessing situations (e.g., What do I know/need to know? What is my journalistic purpose? What are ethical concerns? What policies apply? Who are stakeholders? What are consequences? Alternatives to maximize truth/minimize harm? Can I justify my decision?).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this practical decision checklist when facing ethical dilemmas; it operationalizes abstract principles into concrete deliberation steps and stakeholder analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three general ethical problem areas
rubrics_metrics.description: Many ethical decisions involve one of three areas: misrepresentation of an event, questionable relationships with sources, and favors given to reporters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate stories for possible misrepresentation (could it have been obtained differently?), conflicts from close source relationships, and effects of freebies/junkets on coverage. Use these categories to triage ethical risks in story production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical concerns about video news releases (VNRs) and attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: VNRs are videotapes produced by public relations firms/clients; critics argue that running a VNR in its entirety and without attribution is an abdication of the station's ethical responsibilities because the true producer is hidden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stations should substantiate, attribute, and avoid airing VNRs verbatim without disclosure. Treat VNRs like press releases: verify and attribute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical standards regarding staged/manipulated content (rigged tests and photo manipulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples: Dateline NBC rigging a GM truck to explode was unethical; digital photo manipulation allows undetectable changes and raises concerns beyond traditional darkroom 'dodging and burning.' Photo editors in a 1990 study objected to manipulation beyond traditional practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid staging tests or rigging evidence; avoid deceptive photo manipulation; adhere to standards that photographs and telecasts give an accurate picture and do not highlight incidents out of context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical dilemmas over 'outing' and privacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Outing (revealing a person's homosexuality) raises privacy concerns; debates center on whether public role or hypocrisy justifies outing, noting inconsistency with treatment of heterosexual private matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh public interest against privacy; apply Fair Play and minimize harm principles; consider precedent and policy for naming sexual orientation of public figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Junket journalism and freebies guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Accepting free trips, meals, or amenities (junkets) from sources or industries covered can create conflicts — some outlets forbid such acceptance, others permit limited acceptance under particular guidelines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate acceptance of freebies against organizational codes; when criticized, organizations may reimburse or adopt stricter guidelines. Consider public perception and conflicts of interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surveyed attitudes and allowable practices (empirical snapshot)
rubrics_metrics.description: Survey findings show varying approval rates for ethically questionable practices: e.g., 5% saw justification for divulging a confidential source, 20% approved posing as someone else to get a story; about half approved badgering unwilling informants or using confidential documents without authorization; two-thirds accepted going undercover as an employee; differences exist between print and TV producers on issues like changing quotes, naming victims, and source confidentiality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these empirical benchmarks to understand professional norms and differences by medium/organizational size/age; informs expected practices and what may be contested in newsrooms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balancing ethical standards against other values (decisions under competing values)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ethical standards may clash with other values such as public decency, respect for convention, and orderliness; sometimes accurate reporting is sacrificed to these other virtues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize trade-offs (truth vs. privacy/decency/avoidance of harm). Use ethical decision frameworks and newsroom policies to adjudicate conflicts case-by-case (e.g., decisions about broadcasting graphic suicides).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of organizational routines and constraints on individual influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizational routines and constraints may negate or lessen the influence of individual journalists' attitudes, values, and beliefs; the power of organizational routines varies across organizations and is probably inversely related to individual effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess newsroom policies, routines, and hierarchical controls to predict how much individual reporters' orientations will shape final content; greater autonomy/power increases individual influence.
